title: Thousands of “ghost students” use AI to steal millions in student loans, DOJ says

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A university financial aid officer and a student discuss a suspicious email about a loan refund.

script.en: Hi, I’m here because I got an email saying my student loan refund was ready, but I never applied for a refund this semester.
That’s concerning. Let me pull up your account. Did the email ask you to click a link or provide personal information?
Yes, it said I needed to verify my identity by entering my Social Security number and bank details. It looked official, with the university logo.
That’s a classic phishing attempt. We’ve seen a rise in these scams targeting students who haven’t taken out loans recently. The fraudsters try to hijack refunds.
So it’s not real? I almost filled it out. But why would they target me? I’m a senior with no current loans.
They often target students whose data might be in older databases. Once they get your info, they can file fake aid applications in your name and redirect the money.
That’s scary. What should I do now?
First, don’t click any links. Forward the email to our IT security team. Then, check your credit report for any unauthorized activity. Also, consider placing a fraud alert.

You can file a report with the campus police and the FTC. But the most important thing is to secure your accounts and monitor them. We’ll also flag your file so no new aid applications can be processed without your in-person verification.
Thanks. I feel a bit better. I’ll forward the email right away.
Good. And remember, legitimate emails from our office will never ask for your SSN via a link. Always come in person or call the official number.

script.en: Identity theft in higher education is a growing problem, and fraudsters are increasingly targeting federal student aid programs. These programs are meant to help real learners pursue their academic goals. Recent reports show that criminals buy personal information of Americans who never went to college. They then use it to file fake financial aid applications in those people's names. This happens without the victims' knowledge or consent, and once approved, aid money goes to schools to cover tuition. Any extra money is deposited into bank accounts controlled by the fraudsters, and they quickly withdraw the funds before anyone notices. This scheme often involves "ghost students" who exist only on paper, and it has led to major losses. These losses undermine public trust in the entire financial aid system, and the Department of Justice reports that over 830,000 possibly fraudulent accounts have been found. Estimated losses are nearing $130 million, and the number is still growing, and victims often do not find out until years later. They are asked to repay loans they never took out, and this leaves them shocked and confused. The fraud damages credit and puts a heavy burden on victims, and they must prove their innocence through a long and frustrating process. To fight this, authorities are using data analysis to spot suspicious patterns. They are also adding stricter identity checks at every stage of the application process. Officials stress that student aid is for real students, and they say they will pursue fraudsters wherever they are. The case shows the need for strong safeguards to protect students and taxpayer funds.

sections.title: Ghost Students and the Student Aid Fraud Crisis
sections.passage:
The United States has launched its first broad federal crackdown on “ghost students”—fraudsters who steal identities to pose as college students and siphon off federal student aid. The Department of Justice (DOJ) recently charged five individuals and seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from a network linked to Kenyan nationals. According to officials, the scheme relied partly on artificial intelligence and exploited gaps in the student aid system.

The fraud typically begins with the purchase of personally identifiable information (PII) of Americans, especially high school graduates who never attended college. Using this data, criminals fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) and seek enrollment in universities or community colleges. If accepted, aid is first sent to schools to cover tuition and fees, but any leftover money is deposited into bank accounts controlled by the fraudsters. Some even create fake online classroom presences to keep the ghost student enrolled for multiple semesters.

The scale is staggering. The Department of Education has identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts, with estimated total losses approaching $130 million. For victims, the scheme often goes unnoticed until years later when they are asked to repay loans they never took out. By then, their credit may be damaged, and they face the burden of proving their innocence. Officials have identified more than $32 million in actual loss tied to specific subjects and believe the true total is substantially higher.

The DOJ’s investigation was triggered by the Department of Education’s Office of Inspector General, which first detected suspicious patterns. The FBI then traced money to domestic and foreign bank accounts and crypto wallets. In one case, a defendant used multiple bank accounts to receive over 700 fraudulent refund deposits totaling approximately $1,439,548. In another, a single person received more than $1 million linked to over 300 fraudulent student accounts.

To combat the problem, the Department of Education has introduced online identity verification requirements and automated systems to flag fraudulent FAFSA applications. Officials insist that fraud can be stopped without overly burdening the government. “Student aid belongs to real students,” said one official, “and we will follow the data trail wherever it leads.” The crackdown sends a clear message that exploiting programs meant to help students will not be tolerated.

As the investigation continues, the case underscores the vulnerability of federal aid systems and the need for robust safeguards. It also highlights the devastating impact on innocent Americans whose identities are stolen and who may spend years clearing their names.

long_sentences.en: In connection with the arrests, officials said they “identified more than $32 million in actual loss tied to these specific subjects” and “we believe that actual total is substantially higher,” with “millions more suspected.” The DOE’s Office of Inspector General first detected the fraud patterns that brought the alleged scheme to light.

Stamos for the Eastern District of Virginia said that data analysis “identified unusual, suspicious patterns of behavior” that the FBI said indicated “coordinated fraud was happening involving FAFSA.” Those patterns gave investigators “a solid basis and a solid lead to open further inquiries that have led to indictments,” Stamos said.

The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester.” So far, the DOE has “identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts created by using this PII of US citizens,” officials said at the press conference.
